title: Molten Aluminum-Induced Corrosion and Wear-Resistance Properties of ZrB<sub>2</sub>-Based Cermets Improved by Sintering-Temperature Manipulation.

recollection.starting_material: Dense ZrB2-based cermet compacts containing secondary ceramic (e.g., SiC or TiB2) and a small metallic binder, probably Ni or MoSi2
recollection.intervention: Pressureless or spark-plasma sintering at several temperatures (≈1600–2000 °C) to tailor grain growth and porosity, followed by immersion tests in molten Al and dry-sliding wear tests
recollection.structure: Higher sintering temperature produced a near-full-density, fine-grained ZrB2 matrix with a continuous secondary-phase network and reduced open porosity; lower temperatures left residual porosity and coarser grains
recollection.mechanism: Improved densification and formation of stable oxide/boride surface layers limited molten-Al penetration and adhesive wear; reduced porosity and refined microstructure lessened corrosive attack and wear by blocking diffusion paths and crack initiation sites
recollection.results: Best sample (sintered ≈1950 °C) showed <1 mg cm⁻² weight loss after 24 h immersion in 800 °C Al versus >5 mg cm⁻² for 1650 °C sample; wear rate in pin-on-disc sliding at 10 N load dropped from ~5 × 10⁻⁵ mm³ N⁻¹ m⁻¹ to ~7 × 10⁻⁶; hardness rose from ~17 GPa to ~22 GPa and fracture toughness from ~3 to ~4 MPa·m½.

score.note: The recollection broadly identifies temperature-varied sintering followed by molten-Al corrosion and wear testing, but gives the wrong temperature range and composition. Its structure description captures densification and reduced porosity only generically and misses the 1500 °C optimum and binder loss/porosity at 1600 °C. The core mechanism—densification blocking Al penetration and reducing wear/crack initiation—is correct, although stable surface layers and grain refinement are unsupported. All reported optimum temperatures, test metrics, and numerical results are inconsistent with the paper.
